title: not a book
hook: not a book — a scroll, hand-written, read to the end and rolled back

segments.voice: Yesterday: teshuvah, turning around. Your line was turn around. Today, the scroll a thirteen-year-old reads from. Day twenty.

Here is a book nobody is allowed to print. Every copy is written by hand, letter by letter, with a quill, on parchment, by a scribe trained for the work. One copy can take many months. If a single letter is missing, or two letters touch, the whole thing can't be used until it's fixed. Readers don't run a finger along the writing; they follow it with a pointer, often silver. When it's carried through a room, people stand, and some reach out to kiss it. When one is too worn to use, it isn't thrown away. It's buried. Today: the scroll at the center of Jewish life.
screen: `A BOOK NOBODY CAN PRINT.` → `MONTHS TO WRITE ONE COPY.` → `CARRIED, KISSED, BURIED.`

segments.voice: Torah comes from a Hebrew root that means to aim, to point, to teach. Torah is teaching, instruction, the way pointed out. In its narrowest sense, it's the five books of Moses, Genesis to Deuteronomy, written in a scroll by a scribe called a sofer. Tradition says the scribes of old counted every letter. Wider, Torah means the whole of the Hebrew Bible. Wider still, all of Jewish teaching, down to a good answer given at a kitchen table last night. A psalm describes it like this: "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path." Not a floodlight. A lamp, enough for the next step. Here's the part that makes it different from a book on a shelf. The scroll is read aloud, in public, a section at a time, from beginning to end. It's the scroll a bar or bat mitzvah reads from. And on the autumn festival called Simchat Torah, the joy of the Torah, the reader finishes the last lines of Deuteronomy, and right away, without a pause, the reading begins again at Genesis, often from a second scroll already open to the first word. People dance with the scrolls in their arms. The story is never finished. There's a teaching about the letters, too. The Torah ends with the letter lamed and begins with the letter bet. Put the end next to the beginning, and they spell lev, heart. The scroll runs in a circle, and the circle is a heart.
screen: `TORAH — TEACHING, THE WAY POINTED OUT.` · `A LAMP, ENOUGH FOR THE NEXT STEP.` · `FINISHED, ROLLED BACK, BEGUN AGAIN.` · `LAMED AND BET SPELL HEART.` · then, large: `A LAMP UNTO MY FEET.`

segments.voice: Seventy-five seconds, with the bell. Think of one teaching that has lit the next step for you: a line from a parent, a teacher, a book, a text you love. Not a whole philosophy. One sentence. Say it to yourself slowly, like a scribe copying it one letter at a time. Then ask where it's pointing you next.
Torah. Teaching: a handwritten scroll, read from end back to beginning, year after year. Twentieth word.
Your line: the world's oldest book club. Nobody ever finishes it, and nobody's meant to. Day twenty.

howItsDone: In synagogue the Torah scroll is taken from the ark, carried through the congregation, and read aloud in a set portion each Sabbath, finishing and beginning again each year on Simchat Torah with singing and dancing.
